name: Polyglutamic acid

lead: Polyglutamic acid is a long chain of glutamic acid produced by Bacillus bacteria, also found in natto. Skincare brands use it as a water-holding ingredient.
Human trials involve cancer-drug conjugates rather than skin; none were found testing it for appearance.

paras: The polymer is water-soluble and carries many negative charges, which lets it bind water and metals. In medicine it is attached to drugs such as paclitaxel to change how they are delivered.
Gamma-PGA is described as biodegradable and non-immunogenic. Wikipedia notes its medical use is largely pre-clinical, and safety data for topical cosmetic use were not found in the sources reviewed.

lead: Polyglutamic acid (PGA) is a polymer of the amino acid glutamic acid, existing as gamma-PGA (linked through the side-chain carboxyl) and alpha-PGA (linked through the alpha-carboxyl). Both forms are water-soluble and negatively charged.[1]

Gamma-PGA is produced by Bacillus species through fermentation and is a major constituent of the Japanese food natto. It is listed as a cosmeceutical ingredient, and is promoted in skincare as a humectant; Grokipedia claims it holds more water than hyaluronic acid, a statement from an AI-generated source that is not backed by a cited trial here.[1][2]
The best-documented human trials involve alpha-PGA as a carrier in the chemotherapy conjugate paclitaxel poliglumex. No trials found test PGA for skin appearance.[3][4]

paras: Gamma-PGA is typically made of mixed D and L glutamate, while alpha-PGA is mostly L-form. Gamma-PGA is described as non-immunogenic and biodegradable.[1] Industrial gamma-PGA comes from bacterial fermentation involving glutamate racemase and a polymer synthesis operon, and alpha-PGA is made by chemical ring-opening polymerisation.[1] Gamma-PGA also forms part of the Bacillus anthracis capsule.[1]

Gamma-PGA is listed as a cosmeceutical ingredient.[1] Grokipedia describes it as a humectant that improves skin barrier function and reduces signs of ageing, with water absorption up to 5000 times its weight, claims unverified in the sources reviewed.[2]
Alpha-PGA serves as a delivery aid in paclitaxel poliglumex.[1] Gamma-PGA research includes drug, insulin and vaccine-antigen delivery, and it is used as a flocculant in water treatment.[1][5]

No studies found testing polyglutamic acid for appearance, skin or hair. Human trials of the polyglutamate paclitaxel conjugate exist in cancer: a phase III trial in advanced non-small cell lung cancer[3] and registered ovarian cancer trials,[6][7] none relevant to cosmetic use. One registered study evaluated an anti-redness dermocosmetic for rosacea, a product rather than PGA specifically.[8] A review describes microbial PGA biosynthesis and its biopharmaceutical, biomedical and food applications.[4]
